about: The Calvin Translation Society editors' footnotes to Calvin's ACT, kept word for word and apart from the commentary text. "at" is the place in the chapter text (library/commentary/Calvin) where the note was called; a note with "empty": true had no text in our source (a placeholder) and is listed only so the numbering is complete. Not Calvin's own words.

notes.text: "Ab unico magistro," by the only master, omitted.
"Et ultimum bonum," and it is his final good, omitted.
"Generaliter de gratia regenerationis," generally of the grace of regeneration.
"Ex hoc loco et similibus vulgo colligunt," commonly gather out of this and similar passages.
"Supra ingenii nostri captum," beyond the reach of our minds.
"Atqui in primis renunciandum erat mundo," but they ought, in the first instance, to renounce the world, omitted.
"Hac in parte omnes fuisse hallucinatos," that they all labored under this hallucination.

Transpose thus: As for us, lest we be entangled in like errors, let us learn to apply our minds to hear the gospel preached, (a preached gospel,) which prepareth a place in our heart for the kingdom of Christ.
"Ut de propinquo triumpho cogitare desinant," that they may cease to think of a near triumph.
"Quam in edito et undique experto ac patente loco et constituti," when they were standing on an elevated spot, open on all sides, with nothing to interrupt the view.
"Ad eorum dicta attentiores," might be more attentive to what they said.
"In angustum locum fuisse constrictos," were confined to a narrow space.
More properly, For the Lord doth in the law command, etc.
"Communi sacerdotum concilio," by the common council of the priests, the Sanhedrim.
"Ut precibus nostris concedat," that he would grant our prayers.
"Ut quotidiana Spiritus augmenta impetremus," that we may obtain daily increase of the Spirit.
"Ut ita loquar claudicaret," had been, so to speak, lame, defective.
"Atrocitatem sceleris," the atrocity of the crime.
"Ut sibi caveant et metuani," to be cautious and fear.
"Lectoribus obscura essent," might be obscure to his readers.
"Argento potitus non est," he did not obtain the money.
"Quum opera nostra uti velit Deus," since God is pleased to use our agency.
"Medium fuit temperamentum." a middle course was adopted.
"Valere sinamus," let us leave them alone, bid them good day.
There is here a transposition in the translation. The 26th verse precedes the 25th.
"Ut more videbimus," as we shall by and by see, omitted.
"Festis diebus," on feast days, or festivals.
"Excellentiam quae obeundo muneri par futura esset." but that excellence which might be sufficient to enable each to execute his office.
"Ut peregrinas linguas discere potuerint," so as to be able to learn foreign tongues.
"Nati in contempto angulo," born in a district of no repute.
"Quod autem omnibus exprobrat paucorum vitium," as to his upbraiding all with the fault of a few.
"Eam non negligit," he does not neglect it.
"Suis imposturis fidem facerent magi," magians might procure credit for their impostures.
"Ex duobus absurdis alterutrum," one of two absurdities.
"Superiorem communi sorte," superior to the common lot.
"Non esse periculum ne unquam nos ac fidem nostram frustratur," there is no danger of his deceiving us or our faith.
"Quin erumpat in linguae exultationem," but will burst forth into the language of exultation.
"Hoc principium quod Paulus tradit Christum esse finem legis," etc., this principle which Paul delivers, viz., that Christ was the end of the law, was of great force, etc.
"Nihil absurdi est si partem alteram praetereat," there is no absurdity, there is nothing strange, in his omitting the other part.
"Effugium in allegorico sensu captant," they attempt evasion by giving an allegorical meaning.
"Medii stare," to hold a middle course, remain undecided.
"Ordinarium Ecclesiae regimen," the ordinary government of the Church.
"Ad vivum depicta," painted to the life.
"Hic enim erit status," for the state (of the question) shall be.
"Sed qui suspensos tenet adeoque constrictos," but which keeps them in suspense and restrained.
"Alios nullo metu fuisse deterritos quin furiose adversus Ecclesiam saevirent," that others were not deterred by any fear from raging against the Church.
"In obsequium Dei," into obedience to God.
"Emergeret," might emerge, or raise her head.
"Subinde sumus experti," have ever and anon experienced.
"Nec solliciti sunt si quisquam egeat," nor are solicitous if any man want.
"Quorum aemuli haberi volunt," whose rivals they would be thought.
"Ad templi cultum," to worship the temple.
"Quibus alibi magis distracti fuissent," with which elsewhere they might have been more distracted.
"Et probabilis est uterque contextus," and the context makes this probable.
"Eam ubique coluerunt," did cultivate it everywhere.
"Providi homines," the provident, or over careful.
"Populo grati atque probati essent," that they were agreeable to, and approved by, the people.
"Extra eam," out of it, (the Church,) omitted.
"Naturae autem vitium," but a natural defect.
"Ab invocatione et cultu Dei," with invocation and worship of God.
"A nobis povocetur," until he is urged by us.
"Partes nostras non omittamus," let us not omit our part.
"Principio quidem erat hoc clusorium," at first, indeed, this was illusory.
"Si volumus ad scopum pervenire," if we would attain to the mark, omitted.
"Ex nostro stupore," from our stupor, or stupidity.
"Ubi nullus ecarguebat superstitionem," where none condemned the superstition.
"Erectos," when we are lifted up, or aroused by.
"Quodam, ut ita loquar veterno obruti sunt," are oppressed, so to speak, with a kind of lethargy.
"Quamvis immensa locorum distamia sit remotus," although, in respect of place, he is at an immense distance from them.
"Ab ultima aetate," from the remotest age.
"Quanquam nec sic quidem soluta erit tota difficultas," although not even in this way will the whole difficulty be solved.
"Si noluisset causam ingredi," if he had been unwilling to enter upon the cause.
"Quam pro nihilo ducendum sit quicquid decernunt et jubent," that whatever they order and decree ought to be held as null.
"Hanc quaestionem lepide diremit Papa," the Pope wittily disposes of this question.
"Non posse eos nisi ex Dei mandato praecipere," that no command can possibly proceed from them without being agreeable to the will of God.
"Ut illis nocendi via non pateat," that they have no means of doing harm.
"Ne pigeat," let it not grieve them.
"Ut serviliter excipient," as servilely to submit.
"Qui eos ab efficio abducat," which might draw them off from their duty.
"Per summas difficultates regno potitus est," came to the kingdom through the greatest difficulties.
"Sincero cordis affectu," with sincere affection of heart, omitted.
"Nam et externa beneficentia nisi oriatur ex corde, nihili est coram Deo," for even an external beneficence, if it comes not from the heart, is of no value in the sight of God, omitted.
"Adhibitam fuisse prudentiam," that prudence was used.
"Ut communem terrae habitationem, communem aquae, aeris, et coeli usum pauperibus invideant," that they envy the poor a common dwelling on the earth, the common use of water, air, and sky.
"Accedit huc quoque obstinata mentiendi audacia," to this was also added an obstinate audacity in lying, omitted.
"Praeclarum in speciem et memorabile," in appearance noble and memorable.
"Theatri plausum appetamus," long for the plaudits of a theatre.
"Criminis atrocitatem," the atrocity of the crime.
"Veluti cornici, uti proverbio dicitur, configere oculos," and as the proverb says, "put out the eyes of the crow."
"Qui sibi veniam praecidunt," who cut themselves off from pardon.
"Quasi accidentale erat," was, as it were, accidental.
"Intra privates parietes se teneret," as to keep himself within a private buildings.
"Sed quia illis divinum aliquid subolet nostra doctrina," but because our doctrine has somewhat of a divine savor to them.
"Ut de integro violentius saevirent," so that they anew become more violently enraged.
"Totem Ecclesiae gubernationem horrenda vastitate tunc fuisse confusam," that the whole government of the Church was then confused and lying waste.
"Frena iracundiae suae laxare," to give loose reins to their wrath.

"Atqui hoc ordine prius erat, habere boni et mali discrimen, ne temere quicquam improbetur," but the first thing in order was to observe the distinction between good and evil, that nothing might be rashly disapproved.
"Speciosi juris praetextus," the specious pretexts of law.
"Neque enim mihi probabile est," for it does not seem to me probable.
"Inobedientiae et contumaciae," of contumacy and disobedience.
"Pro confesso sumit," he takes for granted.
"Vicissim," in his turn, is omitted in the translation.
"Eadem in parentibus et dominis ratio," the same holds in parents and masters, omitted in the translation.
"Fidei sinum aperiamus Deo," let us open a bosom of faith to God.
"Sed longe diversum praemium hodie reportat nostra incredulitas," but our incredulity in the present day receiveth a very different recompence.
"Quae omnes illorum delicias violenter discutit," which, with a strong hand, dispels all their delights.
"Ex veris principiis perversam consequentiam deducit," deduces a false consequence from true principles.
"Nullosque non moveant lapides," and leave not a stone unturned.
"Ne census ageretur," to prevent a census from being taken.
"Promiscue miscere," mix promiscuously, confound the two.
"Adeo tamen intemperanter se gerunt," yet conduct themselves to intemperately.
"Humanitatis officio se qpud Deum redimere volunt," would purchase the favor of God to themselves by an act of humanity.
"Ac dolerent etiam mali sui sensu; neque enim naturam prorsus exuerent," and were not insensible to their suffering; for they did not altogether divest themselves of their natural feelings.

"Nam mox retro vela flexissent, nisi novum vigorem dedisset ex gaudio nata alacritas," for they would immediately have altered their sails, (changed their course,) had not the alacrity produced by joy given them new vigor.
"Quod non magis excandescunt apostoli," that the apostles are not more inflamed or offended.
"Quod mature nascenti malo occurrunt," that they quickly meet the growing evil.
"Cum plebe tamencommunicarent sua consilia," yet did communicate with the people as to their purpose.

"Quo nominie Graeci nunc quod aliis praestat, et tanquam melius praeferendum est nunc quodvis placitum designant," by which term the Greeks designate sometimes "whatever is better than, or is to be preferred to, other things;" and at others, "any thing whatever that pleases," or "any decree."
"Hac cura involvi," to be involved in such business.
"Prudentiae usum esse patrem," that use (or experience) is the parent of prudence.
"Sic fuisse implicitos," were so encumbered by it.
"Quibus vix sufficerent," for which they could hardly suffice.
"Spartae suae ornandae, (ut est in proverbio,") to adorn his own Sparta, (as the proverb expresses it.)
"Constituat suo arbitrio," constitute at his own pleasure.
"Elegi communibus suffragiis," be elected by the common suffrages.
"Pastores tamen moderentur," let pastors, however, moderate.
"Ad cohibendos plebis impetus," to curb the impetus (precipitancy or violence) of the people.
"Si fortuito quoslibet accipimus, "if we receive all persons whatsoever fortuitously.
"Summa religio ne quis sumatur," the greatest care that none be chosen.
"Ne quis putet," let no man suppose.
"Imposturis et fraudibus," the imposition and fraud.
"Non laboriosa modo, sed obnoxia sinistris murmuribus," is not only laborious, but liable to sinister murmurings.
"Aliud studium, alius fervor, alia assiduitas exigitur," another kind of zeal, another kind of fervor, another kind of assiduity, is required.
"Occulti fraudis recessus," hidden recesses of guile.
"Uno quasi impetu in eum versa fuerit," was, as it were, with one impulse directed against him.
"Quae peculiaris esset Judaeis qui Jerosolymam ex provinciis comeabant," that it might be appropriated to Jews coming to Jerusalem form the provinces.

"Ut quum homines essent idiotae, summos Papatus theologes sola voce non minus quam fulmine attonitos redderent," that though they were unlearned men, they, by their voice alone, astonished the chief theologians of the Papacy, as much as if it had been by a thunderbolt.
"Quam in mendaciis causae suae praesidium constituere," than to place the defense of their cause in lies.
"Non tamen falsis testimoniis est oppremendus," he ought not to be borne down with false testimony.
"Ut doctrinam nostram reddant odiosam," that they may bring odium on our doctrine.
"Bonorum et malorum discrimen a nobis tolli," that we destroy the distinction between good and evil.
"Hoc ab initio mundi fuit ingenium, et erit usque in finem," this has been the disposition from the beginning of the world, and will be even to the end.
"Sed tanum hoc quaerint," but the only thing they ask is.
"Vulcano devoveant," devote him to Vulcan, (to the flames.)
"Et extra rem vagari," and wander from the subject.
"Sedulo igitur inculcat," he therefore strenuously maintains.
"Ita impiae defectiones cremen avertit," he thus repels the charge of impious defection or revolt.
"Simulabant enim nihil sibi esse propositum quam," for they pretended that their only object was.
"Leves et inconsiderati homines," fickle and inconsiderate.
"A frustratione," from a frustrating of him, from rendering his journey vain.
"Ac libentor cursum reflecterent," and they would willingly retrace their steps.
"Non procrastinat, sed moras omnes rampit," he does not procrastinate, but breaks off all delay.
"Ut oblique species frustrationis," that a species of frustration may be indirectly noted.
"Quod liberum relinquo," I leave the point open, omitted.
"Impia et nefaria conspiratione," by a nefarious and impious conspiracy.
"Salutis minister," the minister or instrument of their safety.
"Ingenti moerore confundi," overwhelmed with deepest sorrow.
"Illi Deus gratiam conciliat," procureth favor for him.
"Pro modo inaequali," according to the unequal mode of distribution, omitted.
"Non nisi Dei manu," by nought but the hand of God.
"Apud quas recepta erat illa lectio," among whom that reading was received.
"Cujus praeludium," as a prelude to which.
"Ad annum quadragesimum," till his fortieth year.
"Astrologia," astrology, or, more properly here, astronomy.
"Ad res praeclaras gerendas aptus est," is fitted for greater exploits.
"Haec heroica animi magnitudo," this heroic magnanimity.
"Oppositas suis capitibus," by exposing their own hands.
"Nonnisi per populum stetisse quominus levationem citius sentiret," that is was owing entirely to the people themselves that they did not sooner obtain some alleviation.
"Atqui pessimam et iniquissimam mercedem reportat," but he receiveth a very bad and most iniquitous recompense, viz.
"Quae ad aequitatem revocet," which may call back or dispose to equity.
"Sed horum malorum indignitas illis est devoranda," but the indignity of these evils must be devoured by them, (overlooked or submitted to.)
"Proinde ei probari," and is therefore approved by him.
"Nos ad diffidentiam natura plusquam propensi," we are by nature too prone to distrust.
"Quasi apparitores," as it were his officers.
"Et compactis arbustis magis abundat," and the more numerous and compact its twigs are.
"Inepta esset loquutio," the expression were inept.
"Hoc enim exigit relatio ut membra inter se respondeant," for relation requires that the members (related) correspond to each other.
"Annon quasi fodiendi sumus," must not we be, as it were, stabbed.
"Quanto majorem vim ab hominibus percipi aequium est," how much more forcibly ought man to feel it?
"Perversus cultus fuit," it was perverted worship.
"Sed nos totos exuere," but divest ourselves entirely.
"Subaudiendae sunt antitheses," we must supply the antitheses.
"Longe diversa est ratio," the explanation (of the two things) is very different.
"Nihil... fingi potest," nothing can be imagined.
"Quam alias referri," than to refer to any other.
"Tanta in fingendis idolis, hominum lascivia fuerit," there was such wantonness in men in forming idols.
"De patribus apostatis," of the apostate fathers.
"Pro crasso suo ingenio nihil nisi terrenum et carnale apprehenderent," in accordance with their gross disposition, they apprehend nothing but what was earthly and carnal.
"Primarium exemplar," the primary pattern, the original model.
"Videtur hic oblique Stephanus Solomonem perstringere," Stephen here seemeth indirectly to rebuke Solomon.
"Gravabant," burdened, brought a charge against him, or threw obloquy on him.
"Hunc qui titulum sibi... arrogabant," and arrogated this title to themselves.
"Qui impiorum aures deliciis mulceri volunt, non tam respicere profectum," who would pour soothing wrods into the ears of the wicked, look not so much to their profit.
"Apertam veritatis lucem," the open light of truth.
"Ut videri posset ab eo," that he might be seen by him.
"Subito et intemperanter prosilire," break out suddenly and intemperately.
"In populo turbulento et prope indomito," in a turbulent and almost untameable people, omitted.
"Ut mutuo confecti," that having mutually destroyed each other.
"Per eum non stetisse quominus in sensum reprobum conjectus, cum aliis periret," that it was not owing to himself that he did not fall into a reprobate mind, and perish with the rest (of the Jews.)
"Non carnis nostrae sensu," not by our carnal senses.
"Ut quidam phrenetici delirant," as some phrenzied persons rave.
"Quod autem Stephanum fecisse narrat Lucas," which Luke relates that Stephen did.
"Neque enim Stephanum ignominia notat Lucas," for Luke does not fix a stigma on Stephen.
"Propter ejus absentiam," on account of his absence.
"Velut in custodiam," as it were in custody.
"Ad ignaviam vel tarditatem," unto sloth or cowardice.
"Non esse mirum aut insolens," that it is not strange or unusual.
"Neque enim simplex admlratio hie notatur, sed ecstasis, quae hominem extra se rapit," for the thing here denoted is not simple wonder, but ecstacy, by which a man is rapt (carried out of himself.)
"Minus dextre quam par esset," less dexterously than was meet.
"Quae sanctae communicatione januam claudit," which shuts the door against holy communion.
"Non exercuisse in collegas imperium," did not exercise authority over his colleagues.
"Detracta baptismo spolia," the spoils taken from baptism.
"Inane duntaxat esset spectrum," it was only an empty specter.
"Vult eam ad lucrum prostituere," he wishes to prostitute it to gain.
"Sceleris sui atrocitatem," the atrocity of his crime.
"Quando nullus illuc emergere potest," since no man can rise there.
"Simplici Dei imperio," with the simple command of God.
"Ejus auspiciis et mandato," under his auspices, and by his command.
"Exilium populi," the exile of the people, the captivity of the Jews.
"Turmatim multi ad eam transirent," from going over, becoming proselytes, to it in crowds
"Neminem ex apostolis illi Deus obtulerit," God cast none of the apostles in is way.
"Liberius in otio et quiete," more freely in ease and quiet.
"Si multa eum latebant," though many things escaped him, were hidden from him.
"Ad nos docendos," to teach us, omitted.
"Et restituat in vitam," and restore her to life, omitted.
"Et mactationi subjectum," and subjected to slaughter.
"In membris omnibus," in all the members.
"Per dubias ambages," through dubious, winding paths.
"Ab infausto trocinio," from that ominous commencement.
"Eadum ipsum sympathia tangi," that he is touched with the same sympathy.
"Esse mendum," that there is a mistake.
"Quibus possunt blanditiis," by all sorts of blandishment.

"Quo magis notandum est Anniae exemplum, qui ad secundum mandatum moras omnes abrumpit." Wherefore it is the more necessary to give heed to the example of Ananias, who, on the second command, breaks off all delay, omitted.
"Quin sibi multum placuerit in sua perspicacia," but he was much pleased with his own perspicacity."
"Oculis," of his eyes, his bodily sight.
"Ut totum suum acumen ignorantiae damnans," that confessing all his acuteness to be ignorance.
"Statim prodient in publicum," immediately appeared in public.
"Opera Ananiae formatum," formed or trained by the agency of Ananias.
"Vim et energiam conjunctam," combined force and energy.
"Quasi obruebat," as it were threwn down, overwhelmed.
"Ut apud se non essent," that they were out of themselves.
"Caeco et praecipite impetu," with blind and headlong impulse.
"Hoc tirocinio ad crucem ferendam mature assuefactus fuit." He was early trained to bear the cross by this first trial.
"Dura et aspera Paulo adhuc tironi rudimenta haec fuerunt," this was rough and harsh training for Paul, who was as yet a tyro.
"Se horrori esse," that he is a terror to them.
"Qui sponte in ordinem se cogit," who spontaneously reduces himself into insubordination.
"Id nimiae forsan timiditatis fuit," that, perhaps, was owing to too great timidity.
"Qui oriundi essent ex Graecis," who were of Greek extraction.
"Ex suis provinciis," from their different provinces.
"Ad nostrum agnotheten," to him who judges our combat.
"Redditum sibi vigorem," that his vigor was restored.
"Initium et praeparatio conversionis ad ipsum," was a preparation and commencement of conversion to him.

"Ut sanctae mulieris virtutibus non fuisse conforme sciremus, et in nomine parum honorifico fuisse quasi dejectam," that we might know that it was not suitable to the virtues of a holy woman, and that she was, as it were, degraded by a name far from honorable.
"Ut pura aliquando ad Dei tribunal sisterentur," that they might one day stand pure at the judgmentseat of God.
"Suspensus licet atque... incertus," though in suspense and uncertain.
"Ne fallax sit ac lusoria," that it be not elusory and fallacious.
"Robur exercituum," the flower of their armies.
"Ut omnia profundant," how profuse soever they be.
"Quum tam multa offendicula occurrerent," when so many obstacles or offenses stood in the way.
"Quantus... torpor," how great our torpor or sluggishness.
"Tanta crudelitate efferati sunt," so rage with cruelty.
"Terror quo correptus est," the terror with which he was seized.
"Ex sensu Divinae Majestatis," from a sense of the Divine Majesty.
"Quae pretium illis statuit," which gives them their value.
"Quin aliquid simal... audesset," without having at the same time heard.
"Doctoris partes implet," fulfill the office of teacher.
"Parum rationi consentareum," little accordant with reason.
"Apud quos verbum suum deposuit," with whom he had deposited.
"Mentis excessus," a suspension of mind or thought, a trance.
"Totum fere diem," almost the whole day, omitted.
"Vel anxietas vel scrupulus," or anxiety or scruple, omitted.
"Ab ejus congressu minus abhorreat," may be less averse to meet with him.
"Qui arctiore vinculo inter se conjuncti sunt," who are bound together by a closer tie.
"Quasi legis contemptor," as if he had been a despiser of the law, omitted.
"Quae fulgere... debuit," which must have been refulgent.
"Neque tamen humani quidquam passum," and that he had no human property.
"Idem semper erit finis," the result will be the same.
"Illud arriperet," laid hold of the fact.
"Judicem a causa abducunt," lead the judge away from the cause.
"Gratam habeat ac probet," may approve and be pleased with.
"Nondum tamen soluta est difficultas," the difficulty, however, is not yet solved.
"Solidam et perfectam," the perfect and entire.
"Ita loqui de rebus probe compertis," and so spake of things well ascertained, omitted.

"Quo significat publicam apostolis impositam esse personam, utque ad hoc peculiariter delectos esse," by which he intimates that a public character was assigned to the apostles, and that for this they were specially chosen, omitted.
"Quas petere licebit ex Harmonia," which may be seen in my Harmony.
"Nec video quorsum attineat ejusmodi subterfugia quaerere," nor do I see the use of having recourse to subterfuges (futile explanations) of this kind.
"Ansa praecisa est," no handle is left for.
"Vel potius concisus," or rather concise, (abrupt,) omitted.
"Totum humanum genus exosum illi esse et infensum," that the whole human race is hostile and hateful to him.
"Quicquid Dei erat in piaculis," every thing of an expiatory nature appointed by God.
"Sed in eo nimio sunt praeposteri," but in this they are exceedingly preposterous.
"Quae in evangelii summa praetermitti minime debuerat," which ought by no means to have been omitted in a summary of the gospel.
"Mediatore interposito," by the imposition of a Mediator.
"Eamque exorcismis non secus elici putant e coelo," and think it can only be brought down from heaven by exorcisms.
"Qui ingressum obstruat doctrinae," which obstructeth the entrance of doctrine.
"Petrum ad causam dicendam libenter descendere quum ejus factum improbatur," that Peter readily condescends to plead his cause when his act is impugned.
"Famelicus inhiare mavult," it prefers gaping famished.
"Annon praeponderet cibus humanis consiliis," whether meat do not preponderate in man's counsels.
"Non est quod perversa eorum judicia amplius moretur," there is no reason why he should any longer regard their perverse judgments.
Transpose thus: "And fear, or else contempt of strangers, did cause those who had fled to keep silence."
Transpose thus: "The gospel which was before included, etc., was spread abroad," etc.
"Pauci exules ac profugi," a few exiles and fugitives.
"Evangelii doctrinam sparsisse," did spread the doctrine of the gospel.
"Otiosa frigidaque notitia," an idle and frigid knowledge.
"Verum fuisse fontem ex quo primum fluxit Christanismus," was the true fountain from which Christianity did first flow.
"Passim occurrunt," everywhere occur, are everywhere mentioned.
"In duces et capita animadverti solet," punishment is usually inflicted on the heads and captains.
"Ad diem festum," to the feast, or festival.
"In prima acie," in the front rank, the van.
"Nihil Herocli fuisse minus in animo," that there was nothing Herod less intended.
"Extemplo ad Supplicium rapi," that they should he immediately dragged off to execution.
"Ut solus emineat," that he alone may have the pre eminence.
"Quibus obrepere suspieio poterat," who might be led to suspect.
"Sed longa aliud fnit Dei consilium," but very different was the purpose of God.
"Ut pacis esset interpres," to intercede for peace.
"Liberalis et regia castigatio," a dignified and royal chastisement.
"Enim consilium Lucae fuit," for it was the purpose of God.
"Divinitus vocatum esse eum de quo agitur," that he of whom we treat (whose election is in question) is divinely called.
"Tergiversandi causa," for the sake of tergiversation.
"Hypostasin non designet," does not designate a hypostasis.
"Inepta et absurda erit loqutio, quod Spiritus Sanctus dixerit," the expression, "that the Holy Spirit said," will be absurd and inept.
"Ut det pares servis suis humeros," that he may make the shoulders of his servants equal to the burden, may fit them for the office.
"Ita nulla ratio prohibuit quin Judaeis promiscue et Gentibus operam suam conferrent," so nothing prevented them from bestowing their labor promiscuously on Jews and Gentiles.
"Nam ut non semper et ubique praesto sint magi qui negotium nobis facessant," for though magicians are not always and everywhere present to give us trouble.
"Usque ad summum fervorem efferamur, "let us be carried even to the highest pitch of fervour.
"Ad plagam infligendam," for inflicting a blow.
"Nihil se minus captare," that there is nothing he less desires.
"Plusquam ferrea," more than that of iron.
"Torvis aut lusciosis," with stern or purblind eyes.
"Sicut alibi, quum dicit, absconditam esse mundi principibus evangelii sapientiam," as elsewhere, when he says, That the wisdom of the gospel was hid from the princes of the world, omitted.
"Larvatos Ecclesiae praesules," pretended prelates of the Church.
"Se adjungerent socios," join themselves as associates.
"Nisi sua infidelitate degenerent." unless they degenerate through their own infidelity.
"Sed in ea re non est multum momenti," but the point is not of much importance.
"Tametsi probabilis est," though it is probable.
"Cujus manu in ea, tanquam in statione, ad tempus locati sunt," by whose hand they are placed in it for a time, as at a station.
"Re ipsa impios coarguit," convicts the wicked by the reality.
"Intermedio Sabbatho," in the interval between the Sabbaths.
"In illud praecipitium ruamus," we rush instantly over that precipice.

"Cur ergo nunc demum ad gentes se convertit, quasi earurn vocatio ex electi populi infidelitate pendeat," why then does he now only turn to the Gentiles, as if their calling depended on the infidelity of the chosen people? omitted.
"Athletas in arenam," as wrestlers into the arena.
"Inanes virtutum larvae." empty masks or shows of virtue.
"Histrionici Dei cultores," histrionic worshippers of God.
"Si quis homicida," if any murderer, omitted.
"Verum quamvis duciter accepti," but however harshly they were received.
"Quod Lucas nunc prosequitur," as Luke now relates in detail.
"Ut invidiam fugitent, aut periculem formident," from shunning envy, or dreading danger.
"Nisi liabellis illis accensae fuissent ad resistendum," had not these like fans kindled their resistance.
"Dux esset sormonis," took the lead in speaking.
"Numen quodlibet. a se confictum," any kind of deity reigned by themselves.
"Originem a veritate duxerant," had derived their origin from truth.
"Non fuisse de nihilo confictum," was not reigned without some foundation.
"Ubi ad infideles transiit," when it was transmitted to unbelievers, the heathen.
"Verbis non contenti," not contented with words.
"Quam vivos et spitantes homines," than living, breathing men.
"Sic Galli sacrifici magnae Cybeles caelibatum genuerunt," so the priests of Gaul gave rise to the celibacy of great Cybele.
"Pantheo successit Pantagion," Pantagion (All Saints) succeed Pantheon, (All Gods.)
"Debere praejudicium fieri," that any thing should be prejudged, (any judgment should be founded on.)
"Nullum sibi debere culpam imputari," that no blame ought to be imputed to them
"Sed quam libet simus restricti," but however we may be restrained (in ourselves.)
"Sed etiam cure impetu irruisse in turbam," but also rushed impetuously among the multitude.
"Quin tumultuose in eum insurrexeret vulgus," that the mob rose tumultuously against him.
"De ejus vita sollicitos," were anxious for his life.
"Optimum est non nasci; proximum vero, quam citissime mori," the best thing is not to be born; the next best to die as soon as possible.
"Austerior est ac durior," he is more harsh and austere.
"Maxime uruntur," they are most of all stung by. The translator appears to have read "utuntur."
"Communicant cum Christo," make them to be partakers with Christ.
"Aut saltem paucis," or at least a few.
"An soli hoc privato officio faciunt," do they alone do this by their peculiar office?
"Omnium suffragiis," by the suffrages of all.
"Plebi electionem permitti," election to be given (left) to the people.
"Adduntur jejunia, tamquam adminicula," fastings are added as helps.
"Nisi quatenus alio refertur," except in so far as it has reference to something else.
"Cura et labore," by their care and labour.
"Plus tamen et intestinis dissidiis est periculi ne anlmos nostros frangant vel debilitent," yet there is more danger in intestine dissensions, lest they weaken or dispirit us.
"Certum quidem est, sicuti unus est Deus, ita unam esse ejus veritatem," it is certain, indeed, that as God is one, so also his truth is one.
"Communis regulae praejudicium," be not prejudged as a common rule.
"Apostolis nihil minus esse in animo," that the very last thing the apostles meant was.
"Ad rem ipsam quaerendam accedere," to enter upon the investigation.
"Quam ut classicum protinus caniant," than forthwith to blow the trumpet.
"Nihil se morari apostolos," that he cared not for the apostles.
"Ventosis suis clamoribus," with their vain clamor.
"Quanta confidentia, quale supercilium," how confident, how supercilious.
"Quos illic imbiberunt mores," the habits which they contracted there.
"Sicut magis idonei erant cognitores," as they were more apt to take cognisance of it.
"Ne inter eos quidem statim convenire potuit," not even could they come instantly to an agreement.
"Dei imperio acquiescere," to aequiesce in the command of God.
"In medio nostri," in the midst of us.
"Quae nobis occulta est," which is hidden from us.
"Ad coeleste tribunal," to the heavenly tribunal.
"Eum opponit," he opposes him to, or contrasts him with.
"Utrosque pariter allectos esse," that both were in like manner allured.
"Nihil esse absurdi si finem... imposuerit," there is no absurdity in his having put an end to.
"Ad necessitatem servandae logis," to a necessity of observing the law.
"In horrendae desperationis abyssum," in the abyss of horrible despair.
"Sed ad inchoandum prorsus nulla," but that he shall have no power at all to begin.
"Ut sui anathematis fulmen Petro et Paulo infligeret," to thunder out an anathema against Peter and Paul.
"Verum quia legis officium est." but because it is the office of the law. Omitted.
"Vel severo et implacabili judice," or a severe and implacable judge.
"Sibi praesse," to take precedence of him.

"Hunc enim finem inter alios habebant ceremoniae, ut sanctum Dei populum a profanis Gentilus discernerent; nunc sublato discrimine, ceremonias quoque abrogari convenit," for ceremonies had this, among other ends, that they might distinguish the holy people of God from the profane Gentiles; the distinction being now removed, ceremonies must also be abolished. The whole of this passage is omitted in the translation.
"Quaedam erat desperationis materia," was a kind of material for despair.
"Ex contempto et ignobili trunco," from an ignoble and despised trunk.
"In ejus obsequium conveniant," may accord in obeying him.
"Omnes ad unum," all to a man.
"Ab ultima aeternitate," from the remotest eternity
"Qui non soldant foedus percutere," who were not accustomed to enter into any covenant.
"Qui non prorsus erant degeneres," who were not wholly degenerate.
"In eo nihil absurdi," in that there is an absurdity.
"Et horrendum semel fieri ultorem," and that he will one day take fearful vengeance on them.
"Quam retuli," to which I have referred
"Nempe, vitandae ambiguitatis causa," namely, for the purpose of avoiding ambiguity.

"Prudenter vero Apostoli et Presbyteri Judam et Silam mittendos censuerunt, quo res minus suspecta esset," but the apostles prudently deemed it proper to send Judas and Silas, that there might be less ground for suspicion, omitted.
"Se apostolorum mentem tenere," that they knew the mind of the apostles.
"Paulo et Barnabas aspergeri," to asperse Paul and Barnabas.
"Nihil a tumultuosis et phreneticis, nihil a gladiatoribus differrent," should differ in no respect from tumultuous and frenzied men, or from gladiators.
"Ex sua umbra et deliciis prodierant," had come forth from their luxurious retirement.
"Seque eo dictante statuisse quod scribunt," and that which they write was resolved on his dictation
"Nihil minus in animo illis fuisse," that the last thing they meant was to.
"Parum opportune interpositum esset," should have been inappropriately interposed.
"Intentos fuisse ad docendum, et in hoc opere assiduos," were intent on teaching, and assiduous in the work.
"Quantum habeant momenti primariae ecclesiae," how great weight principal churches have.
"Subinde lasciviant," do every now and then wanton.
"Nimio Pauli rigori," on Paul's excessive rigor.
"Celebre erat Ecclesiae hospitium," was celebrated for its hospitality to the Church.
"Ejus operam respui," that his assistance should be spurned away.
"Speciosum colorem... cur ignoscat," a specious excuse for pardoning him.
"Locum adhuc habere apud Judaeos," is still binding on the Jews.
"Obstructos esse Christo ingressus," that the entrance of Christ was hindered.
"Literalis," literal, (gone no farther than the letter.)
"Egit igitur callido artificio aliam personam quam ferret ejus natura," there with cunning artifice he played a character different from that which naturally belonged to him.
"Quasi per cuniculos obrepit," creeps in as if by burrowing.
"Hic diversam rationem," that here there was a different reason.
"Colludere puellae daemonum cum Paulo," that the demon of the damsel was in collision with Paul.
"Sed recidisset in merum ludibrium," but became a mere laughing-stock.
"Opponit Christum daemoni," he opposes Christ to the demon.
"Acerrimi zelotae legis suae," the fiercest zealots for their law.
"Tertiam calumniam ex crimine seditionis concinnant," they concoct a third calamny out of the charge of sedition.
"Et alios quosvis sceleratos," and villains of any description.
"Ne quis esset usus," that there might be no use.
"Pedem loco non movit," he did not stir a foot from the place.
"Quam miraculo praeparatus," than prepared by the miracle.
"Sprevisset igitur alto animo," hence he might have shown high contempt for.
"Aliqua consternatione tanget," or throw us into consternation.
"Nec sereno gaudio potiuntur," nor do they obtain serene joy.
"Ad mansuetudinem et sanam mentem," to mildness and a sound mind.
"Si non pergant usque in illos esse injusti et crudeles," if they do not persist to the last in injustice and cruelty towards them.
"Aliquid levationis in posterum afferret," produce some alleviation in future.
"Quia illos jam sibi tenebat obnoxios," because he now had them in his power.
"Nulla interposita cognitione," without any previous cognisance.
"In officiis pictatis," in offices of piety.
"Valet inter nos," is held good among us.
"Necesse fuisset altius sumere exordium," it would have been necessary to go farther back with his exordium.
"Dispersum fuisse aliquod prelatis semen," some seed of piety was spread.
"Hoc compendio," by this compendious argument, viz.
"Qualemcunque Dei cultum," any kind of divine worship.
"Operam suam locare," hire out their assistance in.
"Donec ad vim inferendam sufficerent," until they were able to offer violence.
"Ut homines ad mutuous conflictus accendat," that it may inflame men to mutual conflict.
"Ad se benigne invitet," benignity invite us to himself.

"Sed colorem hunc malitiose obtendunt quaerendae invidiae causa. Non tanti erat apud Macedones religio, praesertim Judaica, ut ejus causa homines ignotos, protinus ad caedem raperent;" but maliciously use this pretext for the purpose of producing obloquy. There was not so much religion, especially Jewish, among the Macedonians, that for its sake they would hurry off strangers to execution. Omitted.
"Nec suscipitur causae cognitio," nor do theytake cognisance of the cause.
"Quae Latinis auribus esset durior," which would have sounded harsher to Latin ears.
"Nobiles et plebeios," that nobles and plebeians.
"Initio a promptitudine," at the commencement for promptitude or readiness.
"Proprio carnis sensu," our own carnal sense.
"Caeco levitatis impetu," with a blind and giddy impulse.
"Qualiter initiati fuerint Christo," how they were initiated in Christ.
"Quod nolint sine profectu tumultuare," that they are unwilling to excite tumult to no good purpose.
"Ex diametro inter se essent oppositae," were diametrically opposed to each other.
"In summa potentia," though in supreme power, (an independent state.)
"Deum statuis vel picturis figurare," to figure God by picture or statues.
"Tali stupore magis tolerabilis est," is more tolerable than such stupor.
"Indigetas et patrios," native and country gods.
"Nititur et contentus est," founds on, and is contented with.
"An inde sperassent," could they have hoped?
"Pro sensu carnis nostrae," according to our carnal sense.
"In ergastulis," in houses of hard labor.
"Familiariter... se insinuet," he may familiarly insinuate himself.
"Aliquo Dei sensu imbuti sunt," are imbued with some knowledge of God
"Ex traduce Dei," are transferred from God.
"Imo libenter et cupide hoc captant effugium," nay, they willingly and eagerly catch at this subterfuge.
"Clangente evangelii tuba," during the clang of the gospel trumpet.
"De reddenda semel vitae ratione," about one day rendering an account of our lives.
"Per dura exilia," through the hardships of exile.
"Ut fieri solet," as is usual, omitted.
"In suis malis obstupuit," were stupified by their calamities.
"Mirum est unde repserit quod legitur in Latinis codicibus," it is strange how the reading crept into the Latin manuscripts.
"Pro violento impulsu et extrinseco ut loquuntur," for a violent and extrinsic impulse, as it is called.
"Si non annunciaveris ut se convertat," if you do not warn the wicked to be converted.
"Optimum compendium," the best and shortest way.
"Quid illis exprobet Paulis," how Paul upbraideth them.
"Capitale erat," it was a capital offence.
"In communi... licentia," while there was a common license.
"Pacem et quitem fidelibus redimere," to purchase the peace and quiet of the faithful.
"In signum detestationis," in token of detestation.
"Vel inanem et fulinem," or futile and vain.
"Cum majore...virtute," with a greater virtue or excellence.
"Scripturae potius quam hominis laus est," is greater prase to Scripture than to the man.
"Quae esset zeli moderatio," to moderate zeal.
"Illis longe superior," and far superior to them.
"Atqui utrumque respondet optima similitudo et partiurn omnium symmetria et conformitas." but there is perfect resemblance, and a complete symmetry and conformity of all the parts.
"Ut januam regno Dei aperirent," that they might open a dour for the gospel,
"Hac tandem se projieiunt," at length proceed to such extremes that they.
"Oscularentur venerabundi homines," men given to veneration might kiss them.
"Nisi quod statui potest," unless that it may be held there is.
"Quid enim... affine habet," for what affinity has.
"Ut clanculariis susurris in aurem proprii sacerdotes obmurmuret peccator," that the sinner mutter secret whispers into the ear of his own priest.
"Quam dextre accommodent," how dexterously they accommodate.
"Densrios vel aliquod etiam praestantius numismatis genus," denarii, or even some more valuable species of coin.
"De exitu ipsos celans," concealing the issue from them.
"Nobis suppetit facultas," our living is derived.
"Si ex illiberali quaestu in diem vivunt," if they live from day to day by the gain of a mean occupation.
"Tam acriter," so keenly help the meal chest, (larder.) gain
"Hoc primum praepostere," this is, in the first place, preposterous.
"Secundo tandem loco," only in the second place.
"Captant honestos praetextus," catch at specious pretexts.
"Dum privatae jacturae dolorem prodit," while he betrays grief for a private loss.
"Quasi turbas ipsi concitemus," as if we ourselves excited the disturbance.
"Unius hominis impulsu et libidine," at the instigation and caprice of one man.
"Quia proconsuli oblatu erat occasio urbis male mulctandae," because an opportunity was given to the proconsul to impose a heavy fine on the city.
"Spernendae ac respuendae," in spurning and rejecting.
"Perinde agit, acsi se misceret cum mortuo," he acts just as if he were mixing himself up with the young man.
"Quasi insculpto sigillo apud eos sancivit," did sanction to them as with the impress of the seal.
"Rigidus exactor," from being a rigid exactor.
"Ut improborum hominum calumnias refelleret," that he might refute the calumnies of wicked men.
"Quos Ephesi creaverat pastores," those whom he had appointed pastors at Ephesus.
"Longe imparem," far from being equal to it.
"Sub umbra et in otio," when at ease under the shade.
"Debiles et infirmas," the feeble and infirm.
"Nos terrore exanimet," make us dead with terror.
"Prorsus esse defixam," must be wholly fixed.
"Non quod enthousiasmo correptus fuerit," not that he was so enraptured.
"Nec tamen violenter trahamur," and yet be not violently dragged, omitted.
"Ad ejus impulsum," as he impels them.
"Quod deglutiendis tantum ovibus intenti," in that being only intent on devouring the sheep.
"Minus hoc consternat pias mentes," this does less alarm pious minds.
"Non negabant illi Corinthii debitam mercedem," those Corinthians did not deny that hire was due to him.
"Ipsos cuiquam esse obnoxios," that they themselves should be subjected (under obligation) to any one.
"Color apprime speciosus," a very specious pretext.
"Nec praeficerentur certae staticni," and yet not be appointed to a fixed station.
"Jam satis superque admonitus fuerat," he had been more than sufficiently warned already.
"A simplici ejus obsequio," from simple obedience to him.
"Quin amore ad sumpatheian induceretur," but by love was induced to sympathy.
"Ipse est solidum corpus," he himself is the entire body.
"Liquidum ejus rei judicium," a clear judgment on the case.
"An voturn exeesserint in medio relinquo," whether or not they went farther than they wished, I do not take it, upon me to determine,
"Sub praetextu charitatis," under a pretext of charity.
"Qualis ista est quam fingunt similitudo," what resemblance is there in it to that which they feign.
"Quod tumultuatur civitas in negotio pietatis," that the city is in a tumult in a matter relating to godliness.
"Centurionos... a tribuno assumptos," that the tribune took with him centurions.
"Neque enim.... tutum fuisset in varia hospitia passim distribui," for it had not been safe for them to have been quartered up and down in various places.
"Hominum turbam ad defectionem impulerat?" had induced a body of men to revolt.
"Ut ad contumelias assuescamus," that we may accustom ourselves to contumely.
"Nulla disciplina imbutum," not imbued with any discipline.
"Ab ilia genta... originem," origin from that nation.
"Vocem audisse, neminem vidisse," heard a voice, and saw no one.
"Commune documentum nobis praebuit," he hath given us a common proof,
"Non esse omnibus promiscue expositum," is not set before all promiscuously.
"De modo visionis," as to the manner of the vision.
"Sancti hominis pectus," the holy man's breast.
"Mente aliena tam vel perplexum," alienated or perplexed in mind.
"Ut familiariter in ejus sinum exonerent suos affeetus," to unburden their feelings familiarly into his breast.
"Certum qua ex causa accusaretur a Judaeis," certainly for what cause he was accused by the Jews.
"Intermedio illo tempore," during the intermediate time.
"Silentio... quin saltem expostulet graviter verbis cum pontifice," in silence, without at least sharply expostulating with the high priest.
"Eadem omnes intemperie laborasse," that they all laboured under the same intemperance,
"In commune illorum dedecus," to their common disgrace.
"Intestinis dissidiis laborare," were involved in intestine dissensions.
"Per marius tradita jactabant," boasted, bad been handed down.
"Itaque addenda fuit exceptio," therefore, it was necessary to add the exception.
"Nec sapere," and not have a feeling or relish.
"Propriam Spiritus hypostasin... in Dei essentia," the proper personality of the Spirit in the divine essence.
"Ipso articulo," at the very nick of time
"Tu vero ne morem gesseris illis," but do not thou grant their request.
"In mediis augustiis," in the midst of straits.
"Ad ejus promissiones surdi," deaf to his promises
"Si difficilis ad eum fuisset accessus," if he had been of difficult access.
"Suo praejudicio," by bearing previous testimony in his favour.
"Quam sacrilegiis impunitatem dare," than to let blasphemers escape without punishment.
"Odium in adversarios retorquet," retorts upon his adversaries their hatred.
"Tutum... non esse," it was not safe.
"Quae alioqui pessum ibant," which were otherwise becoming worse.
"Tumultusos illos sicarios qui se etiam plausibili nomine vociferabant zelotas," those tumultuary assassins who, assuming a specious name, boasted of being zelotae, (zealous)

"Quae factio circiter illud tempus emerserit; imo ex Josephi historia colligitur jamtunc fuisse grassatos," about this time that faction had broken out, nay, it appears from Josephus that it had even then made considerable progress, omitted.
"Crimen velut ex trivio aereptum," some charge, picked up, as it were, in the streets.
"Nec se ad probandum offerre nisi suo arbitrio," and that they do not offer proof unless he decide that it shall be taken.
"Omne tempii discrimen," all distinction or temple.
"Delatus fuerat tanquam," was charged with being.
"Sola malevolentia impelli," were instigated by sheer malevolence.
"Et proprius quasi manu conserta congressos esse," and came, as it were, to close quarters.
"Tale praejudicium tulit," did so favourably prejudge it.
"Officio defungi," to do offices of kindness to him.
"Vel ut se subtraheret a curcis molestia," or that he might escape from bearing the cross
"Non submisse agit," he does not act crouchingly.
"Ut sagaces sunt et acuti qui jus habent venale," as those judges who act ve-nally are sagacious and acute
"Aliquid procul de ipso subodoratum esse," he had some distant idea of what kind of a person he was.
"Ab omni falsa obtrectatione," from all groundless detractation.
"Jus Romanae civitatis," the privilege of a Roman citizen.
"Quo minus sceleratis latronibus mactandum objiceret," that he did not expose himself to be murdered by nefarious assassins.
"Judicium populi," the right of judging (formerly) in the people,
"Acsi quis fabulas narraret," as if one were telling them fables.
"Ne praasertim ubi jam principiis imbuti sumus," and especially when we have already been imbued with the principles.
"Causae sit infensus," be prejudiced against the cause.
"Ubi in nihilum redacta fuerint," after being reduced to nothing.
"Ad suas angustias," to their narrow capacity.
"Magnum ergo pondus habet ista antithesis," there is a great force, therefore, in the antithesis.
"Nihil minus... quam factum," that he was by no means made.
"Ultro sibi in crimen imputat," voluntarily charges upon himself as criminal.
"Quae mentis sanitatem vel judicium illi eriperet," as deprived him of his sober senses, or the power of judging.
"Malam causam ipsos agere mala conscientia," that they pleaded a bad cause with a bad conscience.
"Ad aetates hoc restringere," to confine this to periods of time.
"Honorifice eum corrpellat," addresses him in terms of honour.
"Res jam non erat integra," matters were no longer entire.
"Nec vero absurdum est," and there is no absurdity in supposing.
"Sponte eandem cum Paulo fortunam subeat," spontaneously shares in Paul's fortunes.
"Latebras nancisci poterat," might have found a place of concealment.
"Navis prodore," the stench of the ship.
"Plurimum deferret," he had very great deference for.
"Quod humano sensu nondum comprehendi poterat," which could not yet be comprehended by human sense.
"Socios naufragii vana spe lactasse," had deluded his companions in shipwreck with a vain hope.
"Nec amplius quicquam sapit," nor hath it any longer any relish.
"In umbra et extra teli jacturam," in the shade, and out of bowshot.
"Omni infamiae genere," every kind of infamy.
"Nam quam difficilis et lenta sit dysenteriae curatio," for since the cure of dysentery is slow and difficult.
"Oblique... trajecerint," they made an indirect passage.
"Praefectum praetorio cujus illud officium fuisse ex historiis satis notum est," praefect of the praetorium, to whom it is well known from history that office belonged.
"Pessimi incendii faces essent," they should be torches to kindle a very bad fire.
"Ita causam suam acturum," will so plead his cause.
"In suo conducto," in his hired room.
"Bellare necesse est," we must of necessity war with.
